This smell startup indicates its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth.
  • “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says.
  • In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”.

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”.

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It notes its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture upcoming scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the tech giant’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko claims. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.).

Industry observers note that the company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

According to recent reports, but not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s substantial claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn't a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”.

Industry observers note that michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, notes the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

According to recent reports, but even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker indicates. “Smell is super complex. Context is very key for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”.

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.

Industry observers note that for that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker notes. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

It has been revealed that “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko indicates. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”.

This article has been updated with an additional comment from Alex Wiltschko.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

Pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

Industry observers note that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

Recent findings suggest that two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

October was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

The October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Industry observers note that pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

Industry observers note that sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split showed up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

Recent findings suggest that the bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state at the moment taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

Recent findings suggest that the bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers right now go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who noted they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't initiative to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK owners in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for Â£499 down from Â£649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from Â£379 to Â£814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at Â£649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

In a recent development, but clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers mentioned the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, Â£150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a Â£1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.

Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.

The prices for one TCL TV were correct at Â£649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.

It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for Â£539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was Â£60 more expensive.

Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.

Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at Â£532 to a Â£699 Samsung.

But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at Â£616 (down from Â£749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.

Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

According to recent reports, all the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.

There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.

Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.

Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.

The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.

A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.

He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.

It has been revealed that will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he stated.

He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the substantial retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

Recent findings suggest that but consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under Â£400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are.".

Latest Update: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
  • Recent findings suggest that the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
  • Sources indicate that to test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

Recent findings suggest that the exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another major provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Sources indicate that to test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

Industry observers note that the findings are striking. They included:.

Industry observers note that “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

Sources indicate that although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

Recent findings suggest that the most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

Recent findings suggest that each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

Sources indicate that as noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

Sources indicate that last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

It has been revealed that the clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically demonstrated up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

In a recent development, the researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

Sources indicate that the blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is finally pulling the plug on two legacy smart home holdouts next year.

Industry observers note that starting January 25, 2027, Nest users will need to use Google Home to manage their compatible devices, per Google Home's support page. And that's not the only major change coming: Google Assistant is also being kicked out of smart speakers and displays later next year, making room for Gemini.

Sources indicate that the Nest app shutdown is another step in Google’s long-running effort to bring its smart home products under one roof. The company claims that consolidating everything under Google Home will allow it to concentrate its engineering, security, and feature development on a single platform instead of having two distinct experiences.

Most users will not have to manually move their devices. Google Home will automatically display compatible Nest thermostats, cameras, doorbells, Nest Protect smoke and CO alarms, and Nest x Yale locks. Existing settings, schedules, and camera video history will also carry over.

Recent findings suggest that but video clips you’ve saved in the Nest web app won’t automatically transfer. Google recommends that before Jan. 25, users go to home.nest.com and use its one-click Download All option to save anything worth keeping.

There is also a separate deadline for migrating your account. Users who keep logging into an old Nest account must link it to a Google account by March 25, 2027. Anyone who misses that deadline faces the risk of losing their Nest account, data, and subscriptions as Google starts processing deletions.

It has been revealed that the Nest app is not the only familiar part of Google's smart home ecosystem that is planned to be retired. Starting August 2, 2027, Google Assistant will no longer be available on compatible speakers and smart displays, the firm announced. Gemini for Home will take its place.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Gemini is able to converse more naturally, understand follow-up questions, and respond to complex requests without requiring users to remember specific voice commands — unlike the traditional Assistant.

In a recent development, google Home also features customizable Favorites, better camera streaming, advanced automations, and expanded Matter device support. Existing customers of first-generation Nest Aware will be automatically upgraded to Google Home Premium Advanced at no cost.

At least on paper, the move should simplify management of Google’s smart home ecosystem.

#2427. Latest Update: Are We There Yet? NASA’s Escapade Is Officially Heading to Mars

Latest Update: Are We There Yet? NASA’s Escapade Is Officially Heading to Mars

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA released its Escapade mission just over a year ago to send two spacecraft, nicknamed Blue and Gold, to Mars.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s an exciting time for NASA.
  • Sources indicate that typically, spacecraft use a planet or the sun’s natural gravity to get close to the planet before slingshotting off into the distance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA released its Escapade mission just over a year ago to send two spacecraft, nicknamed Blue and Gold, to Mars. After spending a year looping near Earth, the twin probes completed a gravity-assist maneuver this month and are now en route to the red planet.

Recent findings suggest that it’s an exciting time for NASA. Blue and Gold, named for the school colors of UC Berkeley where they were built, completed the agency’s first powered Earth flyby.

Sources indicate that typically, spacecraft use a planet or the sun’s natural gravity to get close to the planet before slingshotting off into the distance. A notable example is Voyager 1, which used unpowered gravity-assisted flybys to reach the speeds needed to cross the light-day threshold earlier this week. Escapade did this with Earth’s gravity but also used thrusters to generate even more speed. Since there are two of them, NASA personnel had to perform this maneuver twice.

The other massive win for NASA is that Mars will soon have two additional satellites in orbit to measure the planet’s magnetosphere, which is believed to have been stripped by the solar wind eons ago, when the planet likely had liquid water.

These satellites are notable for being NASA’s first low-cost mission to Mars, costing the agency approximately $75 million as part of the Small Innovative Missions for Planetary Exploration program. It also marked the official debut of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket for a space mission, and the company was able to achieve the first vertical landing of its rocket after sending Escapade on its way.

According to recent reports, escapade still has a long way to go. Blue and Gold are now spending the next 10 months flying into outer space. Their fresh trajectory is set to take them into Mars’ orbital path, timed in such a way that the twin satellites will arrive at the same time that Mars naturally shows up, allowing the red planet to capture the twins in its orbit as it flies by. NASA indicates that both are set to arrive at Mars by early September next year.

It has been revealed that by the time the twins get there, they will have been in space for 22 months. Flights to Mars require months of deep space travel, impeccable timing and loads of fuel. However, if missions hit specific launch windows, they require far less fuel.

Recent findings suggest that this is a well-documented maneuver known as the Hohmann Transfer, and NASA’s JPL has a neat math exercise to show how it’s calculated. NASA intentionally introduced Escapade a year early so that the satellites could hang out in a gravitational sweet spot called the L2 Earth-Sun Lagrange point. This is a point in space on the side of the Earth opposite the sun, and the idea was to have the spacecraft already in orbit and ready for the next Mars launch window.

Once it opened, the satellites engaged their thrusters, performed a gravity-assisted flyby of Earth to gain speed, and rolled out themselves into outer space.

The tactic of sending Escapade to the L2 Lagrange point to wait for a Mars window to open is arguably NASA’s biggest win, as no space agency has ever attempted it. The benefit is that it allows agencies to launch payloads into orbit bound for Mars whenever they have the time, then use Earth gravity assists to slingshot them out to Mars when it’s most efficient.

“With this loiter orbit and Earth flyby, Escapade is pioneering a latest strategy for getting to Mars,” Jeff Parker, CTO of Advanced Space and lead mission designer, stated in a statement. “This method provides the flexibility to launch almost anytime and then use Earth’s gravity to get a boost to Mars, rather than waiting every two years to launch there directly when the planets are aligned.”.

According to recent reports, the maneuver paid dividends. JAXA, Japan’s national space agency, released its MMX spacecraft on Oct. 20, which is within the current Mars launch window and employs the same Hohmann Transfer method to get to Mars. The spacecraft is headed to Phobos and Deimos, Mars’s moons.

According to recent reports, despite using the more traditional method of waiting for the window to open to launch, JAXA’s MMX is slated to reach its destination in August next year, just a couple of weeks ahead of Escapade. When you factor in that Escapade performed its gravity-assist slingshot on Nov. 9, roughly two weeks before MMX debuted, the spacecraft will reach their respective destinations in approximately the same amount of time, validating NASA’s trajectory strategy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The NYT Connections puzzle today is not too difficult if you have a sweet tooth.

Connections is the one of the most popular Upcoming York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

Sources indicate that if you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

Sources indicate that the NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Apple Watch was overdue for a chip patch, with Apple skipping any changes last year and not having any true performance upgrades since the S9.

I’m happy to report that the new S11 chip appears much faster and more capable than its predecessor, the S10.

Everyday tasks on Apple Watch Series 12 just feel fast. And Siri AI, a tentpole addition in watchOS 27, very much feels made for this latest hardware. Siri was sluggish on older hardware in my testing, but it performs much more like I’d hoped on Series 12.

In a recent development, the newly introduced Health Sensing System makes Apple Watch Series 12 better at tracking key metrics like heart rate and steps. But this isn’t a case where accuracy is the only improvement.

Because of the fresh health sensors, Series 12 offers three complications not available before:.

Industry observers note that the complications let you see up-to-date readings on your current heart rate, step count, and readiness score right from your watch face. These are very welcome additions that meaningfully improve the Apple Watch’s health and wellness feature set.

I’ve been using the watchOS 27.3 beta, which adds a new Siri Recap feature for Series 12 models that I really love.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment.

Most of what Siri documents, I’ll never need to reference and it gets deleted automatically. But for those times I have trouble remembering a key piece of information, I’ve found Siri Recap a very convenient addition.

Apple Watch Series 12 offers largely the same battery life as Series 11, though it will last 25% longer for outdoor workouts.

More battery is always nice, but I’m especially a fan of the faster charging available on Series 12. Here’s how it stacks up to Series 11:.

I wear my Apple Watch to bed and generally try to top it off rapidly in the evening, but I’m not always great at giving it much time on the charger. With faster charging support on Series 12, my poor planning isn’t a problem.

#2422. Change these settings if you want GTA 6 to feel like old GTA

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (990 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Change these settings if you want GTA 6 to feel like old GTA

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 has many latest features and updates that bring the series up to date, from the intertwined Wanted and Heat systems that keep cops on the hunt for the protagonists even after they respray their car, to charging infrastructure for electric vehicles.
  • In a recent development, once GTA 6 eventually comes to PC (which could be as soon as early 2027), it's all but certain that a swathe of mods will emerge to restore gameplay elements from previous titles.
  • One of the ways in which Rockstar brought GTA 6 into the modern age is by making a key change to the control system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are few ways you can wind back the clock.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has many latest features and updates that bring the series up to date, from the intertwined Wanted and Heat systems that keep cops on the hunt for the protagonists even after they respray their car, to charging infrastructure for electric vehicles. Still, some players might be missing certain aspects of previous titles in the series that developer Rockstar Games has either moved on from or no longer made the default option.

In a recent development, once GTA 6 eventually comes to PC (which could be as soon as early 2027), it's all but certain that a swathe of mods will emerge to restore gameplay elements from previous titles. However, you don't need to wait until then to wind back the clock, at least to a certain extent. There are some in-game settings you can change to restore more of a classic GTA feel, but that might come at the expense of more convenient quality-of-life improvements.

One of the ways in which Rockstar brought GTA 6 into the modern age is by making a key change to the control system. For many years, GTA players may have had to give their thumb a bit of a workout when they wanted to sprint. By default, the console versions of GTA 5 require players to mash the X button on PlayStation or A on Xbox to help them high-tail it to their destination. The settings allow you to change this so you can hold down the button instead, which is an improvement.

However, many found it inconvenient to have this core movement function mapped to a face button instead of a thumbstick. Lots of other game developers have long assigned the sprint function to the left thumbstick, so you just need to click the same thing you're using to move your character to make them speed up.

Industry observers note that rockstar finally got with the program in GTA 6 by assigning the run button to L3 on PS5 and LS on Xbox by default. But maybe you really hate your thumb or for some reason just really liked how the sprint function worked in the previous games.

In a recent development, to return to the old movement control system, hit the pause button and go to the settings. On the control scheme page, you can change the setup from Default to Classic. This assigns run/sprint to X on a PS5 controller and A on Xbox, with the crouch ability moved to L3/LS instead, and jump to Square (PS5) or X (Xbox). In an ideal world, GTA 6 would have fully remappable controls so you could set up the control system however you want. But if you really want that classic GTA feel, you can at least make this change.

One of the main drawbacks of GTA 6 for me after playing the game for 12 hours is that Rockstar hasn't upgraded its shooting mechanics well enough. It's tough to aim accurately — just ask the NPC whose hand I accidentally hit while we were horsing around and doing a whole William Tell thing. The inevitable PC version of the game will at least let players use their mouse for aiming. However, there are aim assist options that can help in the meantime.

For one thing, you can use a similar targeting option to the one found in GTA 5. In the gameplay tab of the GTA 6 settings, scroll down to the combat section and change the Targeting option from Partial to Lock-On. According to the description, this means the game will try to automatically lock onto the closest target when you're aiming. If you enable the Lock-On Target Switch option, you'll be able to flick between nearby targets using the right thumbstick.

In a recent development, this section of the settings menu also allows you to adjust the aim assist strength to your liking. There's also a Shooting Assist option (which helps with tracking targets that are close by) and a way to enable auto-aiming for drive-by shootings. That said, if you're a crackshot with a controller and confident in your accuracy, you can go in the other direction and select the free aim Targeting option.

GTA old heads who have been with the series since the very beginning (hi!) may remember that, in the earliest games, there was no built-in navigation help other than directional arrows that only revealed you where to go as the crow flies. You had to navigate the road network all by yourself, relying on your memory, perhaps a printed map and maybe some notes to help you get around. Even getting to the location where you could save your progress in GTA 2 was a pain.

Since then, we've all grown used to minimaps and compasses that help us get to where we want to go. Those are often very useful in open-world games, which have grown in vastly in scope over the last three decades.

But if you really want a challenge in GTA 6 — and a taste of what things were like in the original 1997 game — you can minimize the navigation help in the latest title. In the UI section of the settings menu, you can switch off the minimap, compass, GPS routes and in-world objective markers and largely rely on your wits.

I recommend that you don't disable all of these features, to be clear. The world of GTA 6 is vast and dense. Getting around and knowing where to go without using any of these tools would be very difficult. But, if you want a true old-school GTA feel or want to make the game as immersive as possible, tinkering with the navigation systems is something you can try. Unlike in GTA 2, though, at least you won't have to zip over to the local church to save your progress.

Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
  • It has been revealed that the tech giant’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
  • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Massive Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

It has been revealed that the tech giant’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

Sources indicate that but all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the manufacturer’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

Sources indicate that for comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing newly introduced renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

Sources indicate that but even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

According to recent reports, still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

It would very much be in the public interest for other Massive Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

#2415. Industry News: Signal now blocks screenshots by default to stymie AI agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (480 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Signal now blocks screenshots by default to stymie AI agents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The company is calling for a simple way for developers to opt out of AI snooping.
  • Industry observers note that signal views AI agents built into phones as an "existential threat," and it's acting accordingly.
  • The measures keep Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence from snooping on your chats, at least to a degree.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The company is calling for a simple way for developers to opt out of AI snooping.

Industry observers note that signal views AI agents built into phones as an "existential threat," and it's acting accordingly. The encrypted messaging app mentioned Friday that it will block screenshots by default on iOS 27, and on Android when AI assistants try to capture the screen.

The measures keep Apple's Siri AI and Google's Gemini Intelligence from snooping on your chats, at least to a degree. The assistants are designed to help users by reading what's on the screen and pulling in information to better answer their questions. But the byproduct is that chats meant to be private — including encrypted ones — can end up on a remote server outside your or Signal's control.

The move echoes one from last year, when Signal blocked Microsoft's Recall from snapshotting chats on Windows 11.

Signal's concerns aren't limited to the built-in assistants. It's also worried about third-party agents like Meta's Muse, which Reuters caught reading Signal messages via permissions granted during setup. On Android, it read messages from notifications; on Mac, it used accessibility permissions, which Signal warns can be exploited "as a skeleton key.".

Industry observers note that the newly introduced settings are slightly different on iOS and Android. On iPhone, a new "Block Siri AI" setting is on by default. On Android, Signal uses its existing "Screen security" option. On both platforms, you'll see a prompt offering to turn the protection off when it detects either a screenshot (iOS) or an AI assistant reading the screen (Android).

According to recent reports, but that protection only goes so far. If the other person has switched protections off, blocking screenshots on your end won't stop an AI assistant or agent from reading your messages on the other person's device. It also won't prevent third-party agents from reading notifications or digging through files. Signal claims operating system makers don't offer a way for developers to restrict AI access "without making drastic compromises to the core user experience." On Mac, that leaves Signal without any user protections at all.

According to recent reports, in some ways, this mirrors the problem with AI glasses, which can record bystanders without their knowledge or consent. That's led to them being banned in some public places, like courtrooms and schools, and being shunned as "perv glasses." Privacy in the age of AI is becoming less of an individual setting and more of a communal choice, with laws and social shaming being some of the only recourse individuals have.

It has been revealed that as for Signal, it wants a standard, system-level way to block AI agents from reading apps' content. It notes it's talking with Apple and Google and is cautiously optimistic about where that's headed. Until then, know that "privacy" is a relative term at best.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you look up at the sky tonight, you'll notice the Moon is looking noticeably fuller than it did earlier in the week.
  • Recent findings suggest that as of Saturday, Nov.
  • If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Vaporum, as well as the Kepler Crater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you look up at the sky tonight, you'll notice the Moon is looking noticeably fuller than it did earlier in the week. We're still in the Waxing Gibbous phase, which falls between the First Quarter and Full Moon, but we're getting closer to the Full Moon every night.

Recent findings suggest that as of Saturday, Nov. 21, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 85% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Vaporum, as well as the Kepler Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Mare Frigoris, the Clavius Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 15 and 17 landing spots, and the Rima Hyginus.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

According to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a New Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Among iOS 27’s many latest features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces major AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting new features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the update also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

Recent findings suggest that after iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Most customers will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

But the carriers don’t unless you pay them.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple plans to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Cars. Smart Home. Leica-powered cameras. You may have heard of Xiaomi for many reasons, but unless you’re in China, folding phones probably aren't one of them. Yet the company has been releasing foldables since 2021, experimenting with both flip and book-style designs as it dialed in on what customers actually wanted.

Industry observers note that like Samsung and the Galaxy Z Fold 8, that search led to the passport-style Xiaomi 18 Fold, which launched days after Apple announced its own wide foldable. In true Xiaomi fashion, the result is uniquely Xiaomi in both fantastic and not-so-fantastic ways. It feels immediately familiar given its near symmetry with the iPhone Duo, yet it solves some of my biggest complaints with both Apple and Samsung’s foldables.

Both rivals set a precedent that passport-style foldables require compromises compared to traditional flagships. While Xiaomi had to make choices too, it made them in all the right places: battery and cameras. Instead of a smaller cell, you get a 6,000mAh beast – the largest in this form factor. Instead of a dual-lens setup without a telephoto, you get a flagship Leica triple camera complete with a 200MP main sensor and a 3.5x optical periscope telephoto.

However, the reverse also holds true. Xiaomi’s hardware-first R&D focus – combined with its lack of a global release – means HyperOS 4 lacks the UX refinement and Western polish other brands prioritize. To its credit, Xiaomi made it easy to install Google services and the Play Store, and its take on multitasking is genuinely unique. Still, a couple of daily essentials don't work as intended, and power-user staples like a desktop mode are missing despite support for wired display out.

In a nutshell, the Xiaomi 18 Fold pairs the best hardware in a passport-style foldable with software that falls short in familiar areas.

In a recent development, call it Xiaomi’s Choice: do you want the absolute best hardware, or slightly lesser hardware with a much more refined software experience? Hardware nerd that I am, its appeal is obvious – though the iPhone Duo being as good as it is makes this a much closer fight than I anticipated.

In mainland China, the Xiaomi 18 Fold starts at 10,999 yuan (roughly $1,640) – undercutting both the $1,899 Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the $1,999 iPhone Duo on paper before grey-market import markups eat into the savings.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Industry observers note that more frustrating, Xiaomi hosted its global launch event for the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max earlier this week, conspicuously leaving the 18 Fold behind as a China-only release. This may change in future releases, but sadly, the Xiaomi 18 Fold looks set to remain China-exclusive.

In a recent development, pick up the Xiaomi 18 Fold, then the iPhone Duo, and the weight difference jumps out immediately. At 219g, Xiaomi's foldable is a full 35g lighter than Apple's first foldable – and only 18g heavier than the Galaxy Z Fold 8, despite cramming in a massive battery and periscope optics. Finished in a stunning matte Nishino Red glass against a dark metal frame, it looks and feels every bit like a premium flagship smartphone.

Looking at raw thickness alone actually sells Xiaomi's engineering short. When you calculate total folded volume, the Xiaomi 18 Fold (105.37 cm³) takes up roughly 6 percent less physical space than the iPhone Duo (111.95 cm³) and even edges out the razor-thin, tall-bodied Oppo Find N6 (105.82 cm³). Only the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (98.43 cm³) and Honor Magic V6 (102.15 cm³) feature smaller overall footprints – and neither offers the combination of a 6,000mAh battery and a periscope telephoto inside a pocket-friendly passport-style chassis.

Even the wide horizontal camera bar works in its favor. Rather than getting in the way, as some have complained, that housing doubles as a natural finger rest and grip mount, giving your index finger a solid ledge to anchor against when using the phone unfolded in portrait mode.

It has been revealed that the keel hinge feels sturdy and reassuring, even if it lacks the iPhone Duo's crisp magnetic snap and holds fewer intermediate flex angles. Unlocking is fast and reliable via the side-mounted fingerprint reader, or 2D face unlock – a welcome convenience Apple skipped on the Duo.

It has been revealed that there are inevitably trade-offs in a body that’s just 5.02mm thin when unfolded. The stereo speakers get plenty loud, but they lack low-end warmth and sound noticeably tinny and treble-heavy compared to Samsung and Apple. Unlike the iPhone Duo, it lacks stylus support, and its IP58 rating means it handles water submersion well but lacks the full dust protection of the iPhone Duo.

Like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, the wider passport aspect ratio transforms how usable the 18 Fold feels closed. The 5.38-inch cover screen is wide enough for comfortable two-thumb typing without feeling cramped, though it is a touch wide (but manageable) for single-handed use and the heavily rounded outer corners cut slightly more into usable corner real estate than the iPhone Duo's squared-off edges.

Unfold it, and the 7.58-inch inner OLED is a stunner. With HDR brightness pushing well past 3,700 nits, I’ve had no issues with outdoor visibility in harsh lighting.

Then there’s the crease. There’s no optical illusion here, as Apple has deployed. Instead, the crease virtually disappears straight-on, but is noticeable at sharper viewing angles – and sensitive eyes may notice low-brightness PWM flicker late at night.

The Xiaomi 18 Fold is more than just Xiaomi’s first passport-style foldable; it is also the first phone powered by Xiaomi’s new in-house flagship 3nm XRing O3 chip, paired with 16GB of LPDDR6 RAM.

According to recent reports, in everyday use, it is blisteringly fast, flying through camera processing and split-screen multitasking without a stutter. Push it hard with sustained 3D gaming or prolonged camera sessions, though, and the thin chassis warms up noticeably along the upper half.

Recent findings suggest that whatever thermal efficiency trade-offs the XRing O3 makes, the 6,000mAh silicon-carbon battery renders them irrelevant. Endurance is class-leading, easily clearing a day of heavy testing. The smaller display sizes – especially the front display – mean lower power draw, with a key net result: the Xiaomi 18 Fold offers the best battery life of any foldable that I’ve tested so far.

It has been revealed that when you finally need a top-up, 67W wired charging gets you to 50 percent in 19 minutes and a full charge in 50 minutes (with the brick included in the box). A charge rate of 120 mAh/min means you won’t be left short, and 50W wireless charging also lets you charge fairly quickly without wires.

Xiaomi’s hardware-first R&D pays off most on the back. While Apple and Samsung both skipped an optical telephoto lens on their passport foldables, Xiaomi squeezed a 200MP main sensor, a 50MP ultrawide, and a dedicated 50MP 3.5x optical periscope telephoto into the 18 Fold.

As I saw during my head-to-head Dubai Marina camera shootout against the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8, that periscope lens isn't a minor spec-sheet win – it is a blowout. From 3x all the way past 30x, the 18 Fold resolves real optical detail where Apple and Samsung smear into digital mush, while Leica Vibrant color tuning and disciplined low-light metering make it the most consistent shooter of the three passport-style foldables.

The only real camera compromises are a narrower 17mm ultrawide that crops tighter than its rivals and a cover selfie lens that flares in harsh backlighting. Otherwise, this is the closest a squat foldable has come to a true flagship camera system. To dive deeper into the camera, head over to our passport-style foldable camera shootout – you can see some of the zoom examples from that comparison above!

Living with HyperOS 4 (based on Android 17) is a study in contradictions. Strip away the import context, and the software is genuinely lovely to use day to day; animations are fluid, and the UI feels snappy.

Industry observers note that xiaomi's six-app horizontal multitasking strip lets you line up three full-height panes at once while swiping across half a dozen open apps. It’s impressive, and on par with the Oppo Find N6 for the best multitasking on a foldable.

Sources indicate that hyperOS 4 makes it effortless to install Google services, with all the underlying frameworks included out of the box: I have been running the Play Store and the Gemini app on here without a hitch. However, because this device is built strictly for mainland China, several deeply integrated Android features break down in day-to-day usage. It won’t let you swap the default system assistant to launch Gemini, nor change the default browser across the system to Chrome.

Then there are Google services. Find Hub reveals the device, but can never find its location, even after enabling every background permission. The same applies to Google’s 2FA – when you sign into your Android phone on an existing device, it’ll often prompt you to verify with your existing device. On the Xiaomi 18 Fold, these alerts never appear, even after opening any of Google’s apps.

Sources indicate that then there are two issues common to China-only devices for years. Android Auto simply does not work, and like many China-specific phones, there’s no support for eSIM. This isn’t strictly Xiaomi’s fault, as China only approved eSIMs after Apple forced the concern last year with the eSIM-only iPhone Air launch.

Despite supporting wired video out over USB-C, Xiaomi still omits a desktop mode, third-party app scaling occasionally leaves awkward borders on the 4.24:3 screen, and it doesn't support 6 GHz Wi-Fi.

In a recent development, the frustrating part is how easy the fix would be. Xiaomi just needs to follow Oppo's playbook and pair the 18 Fold with the Western HyperOS ROM it already shipped globally on the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max: doing so would wipe out nearly every one of these headaches overnight.

If you want the best hardware in a foldable this size and you can live with the software compromises and compatibility problems, look no further than the Xiaomi 18 Fold. By pairing a pocketable 219g passport body with a 6,000mAh battery and a Leica periscope camera, Xiaomi proved you don't have to sacrifice flagship hardware for a wide foldable.

It has been revealed that that brings us right back to Xiaomi's Choice. If you live in China – or you are an enthusiast willing to import a phone and live without Android Auto, eSIMs, and Find Hub tracking – this is the finest piece of foldable hardware you can buy.

For everyone else, the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 remain the safer, far better-integrated daily drivers – even though the hardware is considerably less impressive – at least until Xiaomi finally gives its best foldable the global ROM it deserves.

Personally, the smaller size, excellent battery life, and that telephoto lens mean the Xiaomi 18 Fold will definitely be in my arsenal during trade shows and other work events, even if I keep using the iPhone Duo as my daily passport-style foldable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

According to recent reports, google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

Industry observers note that the search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

Recent findings suggest that the other big change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s upcoming AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

This change says more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The manufacturer has called the idea “nonsense.”.

In a recent development, the Donald Trump-backed strategy that resulted in a US-led takeover of TikTok's American business has apparently inspired some leaders in the European Union. This week Germany and Austria proposed a similar move for the app's European operation, and now the German government indicates that it has lined up investors willing to fork over as much as €25 billion (about $27.4 billion USD) to finance such an arrangement, Politico reports.

In a recent development, "It's a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business," Berlin culture minister Wolfram Weimer told the outlet. "And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares." Investors from five countries have expressed interest in such a deal, according to Weimer.

In a recent development, if you're thinking, "wait, I didn't know TikTok Europe was for sale," that's because... it isn't. At least not in any official sense. And unsurprisingly, it doesn't seem like ByteDance is at all interested in this arrangement, which a spokesperson has described as "nonsense." Of course, TikTok's US business wasn't officially for sale either. But we all know how that ended.

Whether a similar EU-led takeover of TikTok would actually gain any traction is unclear. The app isn't facing a ban in the region. And, as Bloomberg, pointed out earlier this week, Germany and Austria likely can't strongarm the firm into a sale without the backing of the whole European Commission.

Recent findings suggest that EU officials have raised similar concerns as their US counterparts about TikTok's influence and its ties to China. Last year, the EU fined the manufacturer more than $600 million for breaking EU privacy laws by funneling some EU user data to China. More recently, regulators have accused the company of breaking its Digital Services Act (DSA) with its "For You" algorithm. The EU Commission has told the company to change the design of its algorithm or it risks another massive fine.

  • But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board revealed an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.

According to recent reports, according to sources, members of the board had asked Huang about Alice Huang after The Upcoming York Times first reported in October 2025 that Nvidia had an unusually robust business relationship with a Singapore-based data center company named Megaspeed, where Alice Huang had worked. Jensen Huang at the time denied any inappropriate relationship with Alice Huang to the board, sources tell WIRED.

It has been revealed that after the affair came to light, the board was incensed, these people say. A source familiar with the board’s thinking told WIRED that while these board members view problems of national security as “important” and “ongoing,” the primary driver behind Huang’s ouster was “the lying.”.

“It was a matter of integrity and trust,” this person noted.

In a recent development, in recent days, board members, including chair Harvey Jones, have tried to quell the discourse about Huang’s possible return to Nvidia by emphasizing that Huang's behavior flew in the face of Nvidia’s policies and corporate governance rules, sources tell WIRED. While previous reporting by WIRED and other news outlets have outlined factors that Jones has remarked played into the board’s decision, the primary motivation hadn’t been previously specified.

Industry observers note that board chair Harvey Jones did not respond to a WIRED request for comment. A spokesperson for Nvidia, John Rizzo, declined to comment. John Fisher, vice president at the communications firm Trident, which is representing Huang, declined to comment except to say that Huang voluntarily resigned from his positions at Nvidia.

In a recent development, for Nvidia’s board, the possibility that Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government poses a bigger problem than an executive’s personal misconduct. If she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, the scandal isn’t just about Huang’s alleged “lack of candor,” but a potential security and governance crisis.

Already, the scandal has given China hawks grist to call for tighter controls on US business dealings with China. In addition, multiple government agencies and offices have called for investigations into what the former Nvidia CEO may have known about the firm’s chips getting into China. The company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, has also been called to Washington, DC, to testify, as government officials try to find out more about Nvidia’s possible flouting of export controls.

Nvidia and Huang are also facing several shareholder lawsuits, alleging the CEO and the organization made misleading statements about dealings with Alice Huang and Megaspeed. Other Silicon Valley investors have publicly raised concerns about insufficient corporate governance and executive oversight by the board.

According to recent reports, in the firm’s all-hands meeting on November 18, board chair Jones remarked it was “not an easy decision to accept [Huang’s] resignation,” according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “However, the disclosure of personal behavior and a lack of candor inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and values made this a necessary decision.”.

Meanwhile, fans and supporters of Huang, including thousands of Nvidia employees and Elon Musk, have continued to call for his return to Nvidia. Huang himself has remarked he would be “honored” to come back as CEO. On Friday, US president Donald Trump renewed his call for Huang to have another chance. “He made some bad decisions, but he is a brilliant person,” Trump told reporters. “I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology.”.

It has been revealed that the news outlet Semafor reported that a small faction of Nvidia’s board of directors has pushed to bring Huang back as well. Jones has not responded to WIRED’s inquiries about the board’s reported division on the topic of Huang’s return.

Some employees are miffed at how promptly the board accepted Huang’s resignation, insisting the longtime leader must have been the victim of a coordinated campaign intended to unseat him. “We feel like they forced his hands to resign,” states one person on the business side at Nvidia. “We don’t understand why the board is so adamant about not giving him a second chance.”.

Industry observers note that at the all-hands meeting, interim CEO Colette Kress said employees’ biggest concern was Nvidia’s falling share price. The next biggest concern was the board’s decision to oust Huang. But while she addressed the first by moving up pay raises, she offered no promise on sharing results of the board’s investigation into Huang or its deliberations about him.

In a recent development, “The ship has sinked but there’s no strategy to be transparent about what happened,” says one computer scientist working at Nvidia. “It feels like a black box.”.

Why You Shouldn’t Use Meta’s Muse AI Agent for Shopping Next Weekend
